examples.label: Upload the malicious plugin and pop a Meterpreter shell

notes: Convenient but noisy - it writes a plugin to disk and leaves an obvious artifact. If AV/logging is a concern, prefer the manual theme-editor webshell.

Manual equivalent via the theme editor.

name: WordPress - Admin Shell Upload (Metasploit)
description: Metasploit module that uses valid admin credentials to upload a malicious plugin and get a shell. Set username/password/rhost/vhost/lhost then exploit.

defense.why_it_works: Metasploit's wp_admin_shell_upload module authenticates to WordPress with admin credentials, generates a malicious plugin containing a PHP Meterpreter stager, uploads it via the plugin installation API, and activates it - triggering the payload.
defense.prerequisites: Valid WordPress admin credentials. Plugin installation enabled (default). Network access from MSF host to WordPress.
defense.impact: Full Meterpreter session on the web server as www-data. Enables post-exploitation: hashdump, lateral movement, file access, persistence.
defense.detection: WordPress audit log: new plugin installed and activated by admin. New directory in /wp-content/plugins/ with random name. Outbound TCP from web server to attacker IP. WordFence new plugin alert.
defense.artifacts: WordPress audit log (plugin installed/activated) | File system: /wp-content/plugins/<random>/ | Meterpreter TCP session in network traffic | WordFence plugin change notification
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 (ParentImage="*w3wp.exe" OR ParentImage="*httpd*" OR ParentImage="*apache*" OR ParentImage="*php-cgi*" OR ParentImage="*php-fpm*" OR ParentImage="*java.exe" OR ParentImage="*tomcat*")
| where match(Image, "(?i)(cmd|powershell|bash|sh|nc|python)")
| table _time, Computer, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine

index=web sourcetype=access_combined (method=POST OR status=500)
| stats count by clientip, uri_path | where count>3
defense.elastic_kql: event.code:"1" AND process.parent.name:(w3wp.exe OR httpd OR apache2 OR php-fpm OR java.exe) AND process.name:(cmd.exe OR powershell.exe OR bash OR sh OR nc OR python*)
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","httpd","apache2","php-fpm","php-cgi","java.exe","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash","sh","nc","python")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
// WordPress admin-shell (theme editor) RCE via Metasploit - apache/php spawning a shell
defense.prevention: Disable plugin installation: define('DISALLOW_FILE_MODS', true). Require MFA for admin login. Monitor and alert on new plugin installations.
defense.misconfiguration: WordPress allows plugin installation by admin. DISALLOW_FILE_MODS not set. No file-change monitoring on /wp-content/plugins/.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# wp-config.php default -- no restriction
# Plugin installation enabled for admin
# /wp-content/plugins/ writable by www-data
defense.code_review:
RED FLAGS (source): file saved using client-supplied name/extension; MIME trusted from the request.
  move_uploaded_file(..., $_FILES['f']['name'])  |  extension blacklist  |  type check on $_FILES['f']['type'] (client-controlled)
GREP:  grep -rniE "move_uploaded_file|\$_FILES|multer|formidable|MultipartFile|SaveAs\(" .
SAFE:  extension ALLOWLIST + magic-byte MIME (finfo/mime_content_type), server-generated random filename, store outside webroot in a no-execute dir.
defense.evasion: Rename/obfuscate the theme/plugin webshell and remove it after; use built-in editors over uploads where possible; pace brute-force via xmlrpc to avoid lockouts/alerts.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Sysmon, Windows Security Event Log, Web proxy logs for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response
